Start at https://www.wineaccess.com/ and complete the following task by navigating within that website.

Find the page for the highest critic-scored red or white wine, from Oregon, priced under $40, that pairs well with fish or dessert.

Rules:
- Work entirely in this one browser tab. Do NOT open new tabs.
- Do NOT use a search engine (Google, Bing, etc.) or cached/archived copies (e.g. web.archive.org). Navigate the site itself, starting from https://www.wineaccess.com/.
- When the task is complete, give your final answer as plain text in your last message.

Ask Oregon winemakers their favorite insider-secret wineries, you'll hear the Anderson Family Vineyard name come up over and over.

\r\n\r\n

Their terroir inspires envy even among the most privileged in the Willamette Valley: In the late 80s, Cliff and Allison Anderson found a steep hillside in the far northeastern Dundee Hills. With its slope, good drainage was a given. The ground was as rocky as they'd ever seen in the area—it would require a veritable chisel to plant grapevines in there.

\r\n\r\n

Though the conventional wisdom at the time was that the site was too difficult to plant and work, the Andersons forged ahead. They put Pinot into the ground in 1992, and their reputation grew as the vines did.

\r\n\r\n

But Anderson never became a household name, and that's rather the point: they've long sold much of their prized fruit to esteemed local producers like Bergström, Patricia Green, and JK Carriere, keeping only a small share for their own label. \r\n\r\n

Yet anyone lucky enough to get a pour won't forget the quality in the bottle. They spare no expense in production: Anderson Family moves every wine by gravity alone and ferments with native yeasts, the old-world way. \r\n\r\n

Now, eight years from harvest, this wine has come into its own—and we've got a price on it that's absolutely outrageous. If you love Oregon Pinot, this is one to pour tonight and to lay a few bottles down for later.

The 60th anniversary of Australia’s most famous single-vineyard wine, whose oldest contributing patch—the 0.56ha Grandfathers—was planted an incredible 160 years ago. As always, it’s a powerful, muscular wine built for the long haul, showcasing silky but structured tannins, fresh acidity, and concentrated, complex yet graceful flavours of ripe blackberry and boysenberry, lighter red and blue fruits, earthy beetroot, peppery cured meat and an exotic, herbal incense note. The Hill of Grace vineyard, in Eden Valley, comprises 13 separate blocks, six of which feed into the Hill of Grace Shiraz. The oldest block (0.56 hectares), known as “Grandfathers,” was planted around 1860. The other blocks were planted in 1910 (0.33 hectares), 1951 (1.08 hectares), 1952 (0.7 hectares), 1956 (0.88 hectares) and 1965 (0.57 hectares). The 2018 Hill of Grace Shiraz was matured in a combination of new (20%) and seasoned (80%) oak hogsheads (83% French, 17% American) for 18 months prior to blending and bottling. On the nose, the 2018 vintage assists this wine in speaking clearly of its regional location: raspberry and licorice, coal dust, black tea and tobacco leaf. There are inflections of black truffle and bone broth, which always seem to emerge, however the wine is brighter and more focused than I have seen. It offers a beautiful, svelte display of fruit and tannin, with all things in harmony in the mouth. This is very long, as we would expect from the pedigree of this wine and the vineyard. It is concentrated and intense, sinewy, elegant and powerful—a wine for the future generation.

Ask Oregon winemakers their favorite insider-secret wineries, you'll hear the Anderson Family Vineyard name come up over and over.

\r\n\r\n

Their terroir inspires envy even among the most privileged in the Willamette Valley: In the late 80s, Cliff and Allison Anderson found a steep hillside in the far northeastern Dundee Hills. With its slope, good drainage was a given. The ground was as rocky as they'd ever seen in the area—it would require a veritable chisel to plant grapevines in there.

\r\n\r\n

Though the conventional wisdom at the time was that the site was too difficult to plant and work, the Andersons forged ahead. They put Pinot into the ground in 1992, and their reputation grew as the vines did.

\r\n\r\n

But Anderson never became a household name, and that's rather the point: they've long sold much of their prized fruit to esteemed local producers like Bergström, Patricia Green, and JK Carriere, keeping only a small share for their own label. The 16.5-acre site—planted to Pinot, Chardonnay, and a little Pinot Gris—yields hand-built bottlings you won't find on most shop shelves.

\r\n\r\n

Yet anyone lucky enough to get a pour won't forget the quality in the bottle. They spare no expense in production: Anderson Family moves every wine by gravity alone and ferments with native yeasts, the old-world way. And they made the most of 2018, a warm, ripe, generous vintage across the Willamette Valley—this bottle leans into the year's riper, more generous fruit while holding onto the elegance the site is known for, exactly what made us fall in love with Oregon Pinot in the first place.

\r\n\r\n

Now, eight years from harvest, this wine has come into its own—and we've got a price on it that's absolutely outrageous. If you love Oregon Pinot, this is one to pour tonight and to lay a few bottles down for later.

The story starts in the early 1970s, when Doyle Hinman—a Eugene weatherman and schoolteacher convinced the southern Willamette Valley could grow great wine grapes—planted his first vines in the hills outside town. He was right, and those plantings are now among the oldest Pinot Noir vines in Oregon. In 1979, he opened Eugene's first bonded winery, helping put the southern end of the valley on the map alongside eventual neighbors like King Estate.

\r\n\r\n

The fruit for this Pinot comes from small vineyards near the winery—Bradshaw, Sunrise, and Gelardi—in that same stretch of country southwest of Eugene. The winemaking is refreshingly hands-off: nine months in French oak, only a fifth of it new, so the site and the fruit do the talking rather than the barrel.

\r\n\r\n

As for the year itself, the 2022 growing season was an Oregon classic. It started off with near-disaster: a freak, late frost decimated vineyards across the northern Willamette Valley, forcing vines to grow shoots from new buds and setting the growing season back by weeks. But a warm summer and flawless fall meant the fruit could hang and ripen into a long, dry October—an old-school harvest date with the benefit of modern viticultural knowledge. The results are stunning, with exceptional vibrancy and intensely captivating aromatics. One Oregon winemaker we trust vastly prefers 2022 to the already-lauded 2021 vintage.

\r\n\r\n

In the glass, expect a bright, youthful ruby and a nose that leads with Bing cherry, wild strawberry, and raspberry, with rose petal, black tea, and a twist of orange zest underneath. Give it some air and it turns savory, with forest floor, clove, and a hint of cedar. The palate is where it earns its keep: silky and balanced, layering red berries with cranberry, dried herbs, and baking spice over fine-grained tannins and bright acidity, all carried by a thread of earthy minerality through a long, polished finish.

\r\n\r\n

One last thing worth knowing. The estate recently returned to its founding family and is starting a new chapter under a new name, which means the Silvan Ridge label is winding down. That transition is exactly why we're able to offer a Pinot with this much history behind it for well under its usual price.

A gorgeous, captivating bouquet gives the 2016 Margaux an irresistible allure. Weightless and yet wonderfully persistent, in the way only the château’s wines can be, the 2016 Grand Vin is a wine of exceptional breeding and pedigree. So many wines in this vintage are obvious, but Margaux is a wine that takes time to discover, like a great book or piece of music. Shades of tobacco, cedar, mint, licorice and bright, red-toned fruit reveal themselves over time. And yet it is a sense of total harmony and seductiveness that elevates Margaux into the stratosphere in 2016.

The 2019 Cabernet Franc Force Tranquille is made from 85% Cabernet Franc and 15% Cabernet Sauvignon. Medium to deep garnet-purple in color, it wafts out of the glass with a beautifully fragrant nose of black cherries, red roses, redcurrant preserves, and blackberry pie, plus suggestions of pencil shavings, wild sage, and damp soil. The full-bodied palate has so much energy, with a lively line lifting the intense red and black fruit layers, supported by super-ripe, fine-grained tannins, finishing long and perfumed. This is the first vintage of this wine, with all the fruit coming from Morlet's Coeur de Valle Vineyard in Oakville. The Cabernet Franc component is all Clone 1 on Riparia Gloire rootstock. It is a stunning, more elegantly styled expression of Cabernet Franc, compared to the powerful character of the Force de la Nature Vineyard. 300 cases were made.

A superb and harmonious Hill of Grace with wonderful complexity on the nose that keeps bringing you back to the glass. Minty blueberries, red berries and some blackberries. Heather and violets with beautifully integrated spices of peppercorn and five spice. Graphite, salt chocolate and cigar box, too. Intense, lush and concentrated. This is barely full-bodied but the concentration is simply effortless and the flavors grow on the palate. Super silky and svelte tannins glide through the even and cohesive palate. Persistent finish, lasting for more than two minutes. Let it breathe if you decide to open it now, but it will sleep well in your cellar, too.

", "show_plus": false }, { "expert": { "full_name": "Decanter", "id": 10, "short_name": "Decant", "slug": "decanter" }, "hide_points": false, "id": 16357, "points": 99, "review": "

The 60th anniversary of Australia’s most famous single-vineyard wine, whose oldest contributing patch—the 0.56ha Grandfathers—was planted an incredible 160 years ago. There can’t be many wines whose inaugural vintage came from 100-year-old vines! As always, it’s a powerful, muscular wine built for the long haul, showcasing silky but structured tannins, fresh acidity, and concentrated, complex yet graceful flavours of ripe blackberry and boysenberry, lighter red and blue fruits, earthy beetroot, peppery cured meat and an exotic, herbal incense note. Named for the Gnadenberg Lutheran church which stands opposite the vineyard, itself named for the region in Silesia from which Johann Christian Henschke emigrated in 1841.

", "show_plus": false }, { "expert": { "full_name": "Wine Advocate", "id": 2, "short_name": "RPWA", "slug": "wine-advocate" }, "hide_points": false, "id": 16358, "points": 98, "review": "

The Hill of Grace vineyard, in Eden Valley, comprises 13 separate blocks, six of which feed into the Hill of Grace Shiraz. The oldest block (0.56 hectares), known as “Grandfathers,” was planted around 1860. The other blocks were planted in 1910 (0.33 hectares), 1951 (1.08 hectares), 1952 (0.7 hectares), 1956 (0.88 hectares) and 1965 (0.57 hectares). The 2018 Hill of Grace Shiraz was matured in a combination of new (20%) and seasoned (80%) oak hogsheads (83% French, 17% American) for 18 months prior to blending and bottling. On the nose, the 2018 vintage assists this wine in speaking clearly of its regional location: raspberry and licorice, coal dust, black tea and tobacco leaf. There are inflections of black truffle and bone broth, which always seem to emerge, however the wine is brighter and more focused than I have seen. It offers a beautiful, svelte display of fruit and tannin, with all things in harmony in the mouth. This is very long, as we would expect from the pedigree of this wine and the vineyard. It is concentrated and intense, sinewy, elegant and powerful—a wine for the future generation.
